title: Network Disconnection Mapper
summary: A deliberately simplified fictional network of five regions and six pathways, with four tasks that each need a particular route through it. Students damage a region or cut a pathway and watch which tasks notice. Two tasks have a weaker second route, so some damage makes them effortful and error-prone rather than impossible, and several different single failures turn out to produce exactly the same behavioural profile.
learningObjectives: Explain how a task can fail while every region involved is undamaged.
Identify several different points of network failure that produce identical behaviour.
Distinguish a task that fails from a task running on a weaker second route.
State why a symptom constrains where a network has failed without identifying it.
Explain why localisation and network accounts are complementary rather than rival.
topics: many-to-one mapping of symptoms to causes
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native checkbox, radio and button controls; every element of the network is toggled by a labelled checkbox rather than by clicking the diagram, so the whole tool is keyboard operable. The diagram is planar by construction, so no two pathways cross. It is hidden from assistive technology and paired with two visible tables: one giving each task, the state of its main and second routes and the outcome, and one giving every region and pathway with its current state. Damage is carried by a broken outline and a printed cross, never by fill alone; task outcomes are carried by the words Normal, Impaired and Fails as well as by a left border. Changes announce through the shell's polite live region with a full four-task summary. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers; the pinned primary is 361px at 1366x768 so the diagram and the four outcomes stay visible while the pathway checkboxes at the bottom of the control column are reached. Heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Disconnection: why a deficit can follow from a cut pathway between intact regions, and why the same profile can have several different causes
simulationNotes: An invented network of five regions (seeing objects, meaning, word sounds, speech output, hearing speech) and six pathways. Each of four tasks is defined as an ordered route of regions and pathways that must all be intact; two tasks also have a second, weaker route. The outcome is normal when the main route is complete, impaired when only the second route is complete, and a failure otherwise. Three single failures - damaging the word-sound store, damaging the speech-output region, and cutting the pathway between them - produce identical outcomes on all four tasks, which is the point of the challenge. Cutting the direct picture-to-word pathway affects none of the four tasks, which is the point of the damage-without-deficit branch. Deliberate simplifications: real connections are partially damaged rather than cut, real regions belong to many networks at once, and three outcome states stand in for a continuum. The names describe jobs rather than anatomy, the positions carry no anatomical meaning, no real region, tract, connectome or published model is reproduced, and no syndrome is named anywhere in the tool.
